_comment: Threat intelligence configuration for honeypot hypothesis engine. All recommendation content, behavioral rules, and sophistication keywords live here — never in Python source. strategic_controls keys match OTX enrichment tag values exactly.

high.description: Advanced threat actor with custom tooling, manual operator tradecraft, and novel exploitation capability.

medium.description: Organised actor using custom or modified frameworks with targeted persistence behaviour.

low.description: Commodity or automated tooling — credential stuffing, mass scanning, and opportunistic payload dropping.

strategic_controls._comment: Keys must match OTX enrichment tag values exactly. Values are control strings derived from security best practice — no TTP IDs referenced here.
credential-stuffing: Disable password-based SSH authentication — allow only SSH key login (set PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and restart sshd)
Enforce MFA for all remote access including SSH, cloud console, and VPN logins
Implement account lockout after repeated failed authentication attempts (e.g. fail2ban or equivalent)
ssh-bruteforce: Restrict SSH access to VPN or bastion host only — remove port 22 from public-facing firewall rules
Deploy an SSH honeypot or tarpit (e.g. endlessh) on port 22 to slow automated scanners
Rotate all SSH host keys and user keys following confirmed brute-force activity
account-takeover: Audit all user accounts immediately — run last and lastb to identify anomalous logins
Implement privileged access management — all admin account creation must require approval and generate an alert
Enable real-time alerting on useradd, usermod, and passwd commands via auditd
cloud-credential-theft: Migrate all secrets from home directories and flat config files into a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or GCP Secret Manager)
Assign least-privilege IAM roles — no user account should have AdministratorAccess unless operationally required
Enable CloudTrail (AWS) or Cloud Audit Logs (GCP) and alert on anomalous API calls from new source IPs or unusual regions
aws-key-theft: Rotate all AWS access keys immediately — deactivate old keys in IAM before issuing new ones
Enable AWS GuardDuty to detect anomalous API usage from stolen credentials
Enforce MFA-delete on S3 buckets containing sensitive data
data-exfiltration: Implement egress filtering — block unexpected outbound connections to non-business IP ranges
Enable DLP (Data Loss Prevention) monitoring on endpoints for bulk file transfers
Forward all auth and system logs to an immutable remote syslog server — local log wiping must not destroy evidence
backdoor: Audit /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/sudoers for unauthorised accounts or privilege grants
Scan all user authorized_keys files for unrecognised public keys and remove them
Implement file integrity monitoring (FIM) on sensitive directories (/etc, /root, /home)
stealer: Deploy EDR on all endpoints — static AV is insufficient against stealers that operate in memory
Scan all systems using the SHA256 hashes from the IOC table and update AV/EDR signatures immediately
Review browser credential stores and password managers for signs of extraction
cron-persistence: Audit all user crontabs and system cron directories — run crontab -l as every user and review /etc/cron.*
Implement alerts on crontab modification events via auditd or equivalent
Restrict crontab write permissions to named administrators only
ssh-key-theft: Rotate all SSH private keys across all systems — assume any key accessible from a compromised account is stolen
Move SSH private keys to hardware security tokens (YubiKey or equivalent) where operationally feasible
Audit known_hosts files for unrecognised remote host entries added by the attacker
malware-distribution: Block all download URLs identified in the IOC table at the perimeter and on endpoint web filters
Scan /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, and all hidden directories for unexpected executables
Enable noexec mount option on /tmp and /var/tmp to prevent direct execution of dropped payloads
payload-delivery: Implement application whitelisting — prevent execution of binaries from /tmp and user home directories
Enable logging of all process execution events (execve) via auditd for forensic reconstruction
Block outbound connections from server workloads to non-approved IP ranges at the host firewall
privilege-escalation: Restrict sudo access using the principle of least privilege — remove wildcard rules from /etc/sudoers
Enable sudo logging and alert on privilege escalation attempts in real time
Patch the operating system and installed packages immediately — many privesc techniques exploit known CVEs
privesc: Restrict sudo access using the principle of least privilege — remove wildcard rules from /etc/sudoers
Enable sudo logging and alert on privilege escalation attempts in real time
Audit SUID/SGID binaries — run find / -perm /4000 and remove unnecessary setuid flags
combo-list: Force password reset for all accounts whose credentials appear in breach datasets — check haveibeenpwned.com for your domain
Implement a compromised credential detection service that blocks login with known-breached passwords
Enforce a minimum password length of 16 characters and reject common patterns
data-breach: Notify your data protection officer and assess breach notification obligations under applicable regulations (GDPR, PDPA, etc.)
Engage a forensic incident response team to determine the full scope of exfiltrated data
Preserve all logs and system images in a forensically sound manner before remediation
reverse-shell: Implement strict egress filtering — servers should only initiate outbound connections to known services
Deploy network-based IDS/IPS to detect reverse shell patterns (e.g. Suricata with ET ruleset)
Audit all listening ports and established outbound connections — run netstat -antp or ss -tulnp immediately
tor: Do not rely solely on IP blocking — Tor exit nodes rotate continuously. Block by behaviour (JA3/HASSH fingerprint) not by source IP alone
Deploy JA3/HASSH fingerprinting at the network perimeter to detect this attacker's tooling signature regardless of source IP rotation
Enable GeoIP-based alerting for Tor exit node ranges using the Tor Project's published exit node list — treat any Tor-sourced SSH attempt as high-priority
vpn: Implement certificate-pinned mutual TLS for all administrative access — VPN IP masking becomes irrelevant when the client certificate is the authentication factor
Log and alert on SSH connections from known VPN provider IP ranges (e.g. Mullvad, NordVPN exit ranges) — legitimate administrative users should be connecting from known corporate IP space
Enforce geographic access controls — if administrative users are not expected to connect from the observed country, block or challenge the attempt at the application layer
bulletproof-hosting: Engage your hosting provider's abuse team with the IOC list — bulletproof hosters may not respond, but the attempt is required for legal documentation
Add the identified ASN(s) to your threat intelligence platform as high-risk infrastructure — all future connections from these ASNs should be treated as elevated priority
Consider null-routing or BGP blackholing for the identified ASN ranges if traffic from this provider has no legitimate business purpose for your organisation
residential-proxy: Treat residential proxy source IPs as compromised devices belonging to third parties — do not contact the IP owner directly; report to the relevant CERT
Deploy behavioural detection rather than IP reputation scoring — residential proxies will have low AbuseIPDB scores even during active attacks
Implement anomaly detection on connection patterns: residential IPs connecting to SSH at volume or with scripted timing are not legitimate end users
compromised-router: Report the compromised router IP to the ISP's abuse desk — the device owner is likely unaware their router is being used as a jump host
Add the observed router ASN to your threat feed and alert on future connections from the same subnet — attackers reuse compromised infrastructure
Deploy JA3/HASSH fingerprinting to detect re-entry from rotated IPs using the same tooling — the attacker controls the router, not its exit IP

_abuseipdb_note: AbuseIPDB risk_score is intentionally NOT used to determine attacker sophistication anywhere in this system. It is a crowd complaint counter. A fresh APT VPS will score 0. A noisy Mirai bot will score 100. These are inverted from their true sophistication level. The strategic_controls above are keyed by OTX tags (controlled vocabulary), not by risk_score thresholds.
